newsitem.title: USA: Mississippi judge to rule on Liggett documents.
newsitem.headline: Mississippi judge to rule on Liggett documents.

text.p: A Mississippi judge will decide whether to review documents from Brooke Group Ltd's Liggett Group as part of a $650 million second-hand smoke lawsuit against cigarette makers, state officials said on Tuesday.

Jones County Circuit Judge Billy Joe Landrum ordered Liggett last week to send the documents to his court in Laurel, Miss., where he has been presiding over a wrongful death case brought by the family of Burl Butler, a barber who died of cancer in 1994.
The lawsuit alleges that the 60-year-old Butler, who never smoked, was made ill by second-hand smoke from the cigarettes and cigars of patrons who visited his barber shop over the course of 30 years.

Landrum met Monday with lawyers for Liggett, the Butler family and Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore, who was the first of 22 state attorneys general to sue the tobacco industry for tax money spent treating Medicaid recipients for smoking-related illnesses.
He later issued an order preventing cigarette makers from taking legal action against Liggett for distributing documents for judicial review.
Landrum was to decide whether to review the documents for the case following a hearing set for Wednesday in Jones County Circuit Court.

Meanwhile, the judge also ordered Liggett documents to be copied and sent to Jackson County Chancery Judge William Myers, who was to preside over the Mississippi government's case against cigarette makers when it reached trial in the Pascagoula, Miss., court on June 2.
Attorneys for the defendants were not present at the meeting with Landrum.

Last Thursday, the tobacco industry obtained a restraining order from a North Carolina judge instructing Liggett not to hand over documents that might reveal joint legal defense efforts by the cigarette companies. Moore said last week that he did not intend to follow the North Carolina court order.

The Liggett documents were part of a settlement last week between the tobacco company and the attorneys general who have brought suit against cigarette makers in a bid to recoup Medicaid expenditures.

"This is a settlement I negotiated, and I've got a responsibility to make sure the documents get to every state in the country," Moore said. "There are attorneys general and private attorneys all over America doing similar things."
Cynthia Langston, the Jackson, Miss., lawyer for the Butler family, said she believes the documents demonstrate a range of tobacco industry practices, including advertising strategies.
"From what we know about them, it appears that they are invaluable to our case to our claims of conspiracy and fraud," she said.
